welcome.content:
T
hose Who Wander is a dynamic 
game system distinct for its 
branching character paths, diverse 
and versatile parentages, enigmatic 
and awakening heirlooms, 
mechanically defining character 
backgrounds, and more.
The game’s name comes from the popular line, “Not 
all those who wander are lost,” originally penned by 
J.R.R. Tolkien. In more ways than one, Those Who 
Wander epitomizes the journey made of numberless 
steps. Each step is a decision—left or right. And each 
decision leaves its mark on you. No matter where you 
wander, we hope you feel at home all along the way.
Your story really begins before you were born. In 
Those Who Wander, you choose two birth parents from 
whom you inherit your innate and physiological traits. 
Will you choose two human parents, an elven father 
and an orc mother? Or any one of hundreds of other 
unique pairings? The choice is yours.
Biology is not destiny. The people and culture that 
raised you and the choices you made while growing up 
are what developed and molded you. Your background 
supplies all your learned traits, including abilities, 
proficiencies, language, training, and more. Are you 
an artist or a warrior? A miner or a mathematician?
Like heroes before you, you inherited or discovered 
an object of strange powers. After some time, this 
heirloom awakens, sharing its secrets and hidden 
powers with you as you develop your own.
Armed with your parentage, background, and 
heirloom, you embark on your heroic campaign. The 
greatest journey begins with a single step. Do you 
choose left or right? Your character progresses over the 
course of the campaign using the new step system. At 
each juncture, you choose between no more than two 
character features. But the options multiply almost 
exponentially. Over time, you and your fellow party 
members grow ever more diverse and specialized in 
your powers.
No matter who you are as a player, you can find 
yourself mirrored in Those Who Wander, with options 
for prosthetics and wheelchairs, any parentage pairing, 
original creature and peoples lore, and viable blind 
and deaf heroes. What’s more, player agency is nigh 
inviolable.
Not only is player choice held in high regard, care 
has been taken to place players in the spotlight and 
keep them there with combat mechanics that keep the 
players’ dice rolling and allow the storytellers to do 
what they do best.
Those Who Wander is backward-compatible with the 
fifth edition of the world’s most-played roleplaying 
game. That means you can run a 5e adventure with 
virtually no conversion necessary. If you are familiar 
with 5e, the mechanics presented here will feel 
familiar, but with countless novel applications.
We hope this game, and the worlds it creates for 
you and your party, feel like your own. Embark, 
adventurers! This journey is wholly yours.

getting_started.content:
C h a p t e r 1 : G e t t i n g S ta r t e d
5
Chapter 1: Getting Started
W
hat constitutes a player character? 
Is it who their parents were, what 
they’ve done until now, what 
they carry with them, or the 
skills that nature and training 
gave them? Yes, it’s partly all of 
that. But there are indefinable 
qualities that make up a character as well, things you 
won’t find in any book: it’s you, the player, the one 
holding the character sheet, who breathes life and 
personality into what otherwise would only be paper 
and numbers.
In Those Who Wander, you build a character out of 
five main building blocks:

parentage.content:
“I know you fear becoming what your parents were. 
But we are so much more than flesh, blood, and bone. 
You chart your own course.”
Physiologically, the only ancestry that matters to your 
character is that of your closest relatives: your birth 
parents. Those Who Wander assumes you can be born 
of any pairing of two fantasy people, whether it be 
two humans from a small village or an orc and a devil 
who found love in the middle of an interplanar war.
Your birth parents pass along to you your physical 
and innate traits. Your cultural traits don’t appear until 
you select your background. After all, you may have 
been born to sylvan elves, but perhaps you also were 
adopted by human miners.
Choose two birth parents from the options listed 
in the next chapter and combine the traits you inherit 
from each one.
Your default base speed is 30 feet, though one or 
both of your birth parents might modify that up or 
down. Your height in inches determines whether your 
size is Small or Medium. If you are at least 45 inches 
tall (3’9”), you are Medium in size. Those shorter than 
45 inches are considered Small creatures.

physical_disability.content:
Those Who Wander makes no assumptions about 
whether your character is able-bodied or disabled. 
Should you choose to create a character who is 
disabled, options are provided for Blind and Deaf 
characters, as well as prosthetic limbs and wheelchairs.
Characters who use mobility aids or other assistive 
devices are assumed to have them included among 
their starting equipment and are assumed to be a part 
of the character, so any attacks targeting your aid or 
device is considered an attack against you instead.
At the player’s and storyteller’s discretion, a 
character with only one gripping hand and no upper 
prosthesis cannot wield two-handed weapons and 
ignores the versatile weapon property. 
Blindness is a spectrum. Blind characters have either 
varying degrees of vision or no sight at all. A Blind 
character has the following traits:
•	 Choose a number between −1 and −5 (−1 being 
Blindness that interferes with reading and cooking 
to −5 being a complete lack of sight). Apply this 
number to attack checks and ability checks that rely 
on sight.
•	 Reduce the range of your ranged spell attacks to 
5 feet, unless an ally is taking the Help action to 
guide your aim.
•	 Your primary sense is hearing (while all nonblind 
characters’ primary sense is sight) and you’re 
described as a hearing creature.
•	 You’re immune to visual effects that cause the 
disoriented condition.
Deafness is a spectrum. Deaf characters have either 
varying degrees of hearing or hear nothing at all. A 
Deaf character has the following traits:
•	 Choose a number between −1 and −5 (−1 being 
Deafness that interferes with communicating 
verbally to −5 being a complete lack of hearing). 
Apply this number to ability checks that rely on 
hearing.
•	 You have resistance to thunder damage and 
immunity to audible effects that cause the 
disoriented condition.
•	 A Deaf character is unaffected by the silence spell 
unless they attempt to speak vocally. They can 
provide their articulated spell component by 
using the sign languages they’re fluent in or visual 
vernacular.

background.content:
“I’m a child of nobles. But my nurse raised me, the 
alleyways were my playground, and ever since I ran away 
from home, gambling’s been my trade.”
The people who raised you, who were your neighbors, 
and who worked alongside you or trained you 
left a profound impression on you. You also made 
choices all along the way that led you, whether 
straightforward or meandering, to your start as an 
adventurer. Culture, life experiences, and profession 
make up your character’s background.
Choose a background from the listed options in 
chapter 3.

heirloom.content:
“This dusty old book? Found it in a trash heap. You 
might say it spoke to me. Because it literally did.”
An heirloom is an item—such as a weapon, suit of 
armor, shield, tool, bauble, or trinket—that seems 
mundane at first but grows in power and personality 
over time. You can find the heirloom options in 
chapter 4.
Each time you take a step, your heirloom gains a 
new property that you can use. Check the relevant 
heirloom entry for details.

abilities.content:
“You say you’ve been preparing for this day. What did 
you do? Lift weights? Practice your aim? —judging by 
that crater you just left in the ground at my feet, I’m 
going to guess wizardry.”
Each creature has six abilities: Strength, Agility, 
Health, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Presence. (See 
chapter 7, “Playing the Game,” for more information 
on abilities.) These abilities are represented by a bonus 
or penalty that is applied to various rolls in the game. 
For example, if your character is wielding a greataxe 
in battle, they add their Strength to both attack and 
damage rolls.
Nonplayer creatures can have abilities anywhere 
from −5 to +10. Characters, however, generally have 
abilities no lower than −1 and no greater than +5.
To determine your abilities, you can use one of 
three methods. The first is the array. Simply apply the 
following bonuses and penalty to whichever abilities 
you want: +2, +2, +1, +1, +0, −1.
Imagining Holly as an outdoorswoman, Rosa chooses the guide 
background. They record the increase to Holly’s abilities, her 
saving checks and skills proficiencies.
Rosa records the equipment from Holly’s background: an 
explorer’s pack, well-drawn maps of places she's traveled, a set 
of traveler’s clothes, and a belt pouch containing money. She 
also gets to choose between leather armor and a weapon with 
which she’s proficient. She chooses a dagger.
Finally, Holly is fluent in a regional sign language called Finger 
Speech, as well as knowing Draconic and Elvish for her other two 
languages.
Rosa wants Holly to have a mysterious past, so they choose 
the Orb of the Seer as her heirloom. They record the extra 
proficiencies granted from the orb and list the orb among her 
equipment. The orb doesn’t do much now, but it’ll grow more 
powerful over time.
Rosa has been invited to play Those Who Wander with some 
friends. Rosa decides they want to play a lovable but mysterious 
character named Holly. They decide they want their character’s 
birth mother to have been a dragon and their character’s birth 
father to have been an elf.
Their character gains the Keen Senses, Sylvan Magic, and Trance 
traits from her dad and the Darkvision and Damage Resistance 
traits from her mom. Holly’s walking speed is 30 feet, and Rosa 
determines that their character’s size is 5′8″ tall (31 inches from 
her father, 37 inches from her mother), so her size is Medium.
Rosa is Deaf themself and wants Holly to share their disability.
D r a c o n i c -E l f

first_step.content:
“Right or left. It’s a simple decision, seemingly 
insignificant at the time. But a series of lefts or rights 
leads to vastly different destinations.”
Any character’s first step is a simple decision: A or B, 
left or right, preternatural or scrappy. And each step 
on the path of character progression is just as simple, 
with no more than two options each time. Obviously, 
these simple choices over time have consequences, 
and the characters become increasingly diverse in 
specialization and party role over time. But each time 
it’s still a choice between just two options.
This binary choice makes the game simple enough 
for even the newest of players to grasp: one step at 
a time, even while making progression an integral 
part of discovering who a character is. It’s most 
satisfying when character progression reflects character 
development.
But for now, all you have to do is choose between 
two options and record the accompanying feature and 
Health Die on your character sheet.

equipment.content:
“Now, I can see you don’t have much coin on you. Not 
to worry, young miss. I know you’re good for it, and we 
can always just borrow against your family’s estate.”
In addition to your heirloom and the starting 
equipment from your background, you may wish to 
buy additional equipment. In order to do that, you 
need to reference your wealth score.
Which background you choose determines 
your starting wealth score. Your wealth score is an 
approximate measure of the coin, barterable goods, 
and credit at your character’s disposal. Most characters 
start with a wealth score of 1.
When making a purchase, if the item’s value score is 
lower than your wealth score, you can buy the item. If 
the value score is equal to your wealth score, you can 
still make the purchase, but the item or service is so 
costly that doing so lowers your wealth score by 1. If 
the value score is greater than your wealth score, the 
price is so prohibitively high that you cannot buy it 
without first raising your wealth score.

come_together.content:
Don’t go it alone. Your character can team up with 
other players’ characters to form an adventuring party. 
Make sure that the group’s goals and values have 
enough overlap to keep the party together.

worldbuilding.content:
The first time you sit down with your fellow players, 
you should together come up with a campaign premise 
everyone at the table is happy with. Coming up with 
a campaign can be a collaborative activity that often 
starts with the storyteller, though anyone can take 
initiative on this.
Some start like J.R.R. Tolkien, who created a 
fictional language or two first and then began writing 
creation myths and detailed histories of his fantasy 
setting. That’s known as the top-down approach. The 
approach starts with the big picture and then works 
its way down. That approach can be overwhelming to 
new storytellers, so another option is to go bottom-
Rosa wants Holly to be a mysterious and insightful spellcaster, 
so they make her highest ability Presence, followed by Wisdom. 
Holly is also nimble and hardy, so her Agility and Health abilities 
are the next highest abilities. They round out Holly’s abilities 
with Intelligence next and Strength as the lowest.
Holly’s abilities look like this: Strength −1, Agility +1, Health +1, 
Intelligence +0, Wisdom +2, Presence +2.
Rosa wants Holly to become a powerful spellcaster. The Orb of 
the Seer was a good choice for this theme, and Rosa augments 
it by choosing preternatural as Holly’s first step. They record 
Holly’s cantrips and spells on their character sheet and choose 
Presence as her spellcasting ability.
Holly has a starting wealth score of 1, meaning she can obtain 
as many items with a value score of 0 as she wants and a single 
item with a value score of 1. She purchases darts, with a value 
score of 0, without lowering her wealth score. But purchasing 
a spear, with a value score of 1, lowers her wealth score by 0, 
leaving her broke.

givennew_method.content:
The basic idea of the given-new method is that, before 
introducing new information, it’s best to bring to 
mind what people have heard before. This is what 
fleshes out the campaign world without having to be 
detailed.
Most players already have a mental library of 
fantasy and sci-fi tropes. They've watched The Lord of 
the Rings or Star Wars, read Earthsea or Ender’s Game, 
or collected comic books or manga. When you say, 
“Let’s play an epic fantasy game,” they already have an 
idea of what that might involve.
It might be tempting, when building a new 
campaign setting, to throw something completely new 
at your fellow players. But a totally unfamiliar world is 
disorienting for players and a lot of unnecessary work 
for storytellers who have to build literally everything 
from scratch.
Still, you wouldn’t be building a new campaign 
setting if middle-age Earth worked just fine. You want 
to create something different, something new.
If you want your fellow players to hit the ground 
running while still flexing your creative muscles, give 
them a mix of the familiar (the given) and your own 
spin (the new). The general rule is one given and at 
least two news. For example, you can say you want 
a medieval fantasy setting, but the beasts of burden, 
pets, and mounts are all dinosaurs and a pantheon of 
gods personally rule separate city-states.
Before or during that first meeting, write down 
what your campaign setting is most like and two or 
three important ways it’s original. This is your pitch.

the_pitch.content:
Unless you’re planning on live-streaming your 
campaign setting, you have one very specific audience 
in mind: your fellow players. Once you’ve written 
your pitch, it’s time to throw it to them.
It’s like you’re a writer pitching to a 
publisher. If your fellow players don’t 
like your pitch, go back to the drawing 
board or pitch it to a different group. 
Eventually, you’ll find a pitch your group 
likes or a group who likes your pitch. When you’ve 
found a match, you can begin the next step.

the_spotlight.content:
Unlike fantasy authors, you don’t create every 
character in the story. Each of the players plays one 
hero. The storyteller is everything else.
Before going further, storytellers should ask each 
player what character they want to play in your 
setting. Upon hearing the pitch, many players already 
have a rough idea of who they want to play. A good 
pitch usually sets their imaginations loose. Storytellers 
should find out everything they can about who the 
players want to play. Their answers are the story seeds 
the storytellers can use to worldbuild.
For example, if a player says, “I want to play the 
brash, illegitimate daughter of the king,” you need to 
create a kingdom and a king.
“I want to play a detective with amnesia about the 
last few weeks.” You need to create a compelling story 
about what transpired during that bout of amnesia.
“I want to be a priest devoted to the god of love.” 
If there’s no god of love in your setting, make one. Or 
have the player do it.
Make sure there is room in the world for the kinds 
of characters the players want to play. If the pitch 
is that there are talking dinosaurs in your setting, a 
player might really gravitate toward that idea. That

safety_tools.content:
We strongly encourage using safety tools to make the 
game a fun and rewarding experience for everyone at 
the table. Generally, foster a culture of communication 
and trust at your table. This starts with valuing the 
enjoyment and well-being of others as much as you 
value your own. And be ready and willing to change 
aspects of the campaign that really aren’t working for 
one or more people at your table.
Be sure that when establishing safety tools you do 
not press for details by asking or even wondering 
aloud why, for example, a player has arachnophobia. 
No one owes you their trauma.
Film Analogy
One safety tool is to treat the game a bit like a movie 
player. Do this by, first of all, establishing a content 
rating you can all agree on. Just as movies have ratings 
(Adult, Teen, Kids, etc.), so too can your game. 
You can even establish levels for different kinds of 
content. For example, maybe your group is okay with 
adult-level violence, but the sexual content is set to 
just teen-level. Or vice versa. Make sure everyone is 
comfortable with the rating. Setting a content rating 
frees the storyteller and players to push the game in 
any pre-approved direction confident that everyone is 
on board and it’s not crossing any line.
Of course, not everything can be anticipated before 
the game begins. Accordingly, the movie analogy can 
come into play mid-session as well. Give fellow players 
the ability to Rewind, Pause, Resume, or Fast Forward 
the game. During a session, storytellers or players can 
say these commands aloud or tap a prepared card.
Rewind (<<). The rewind command is used when 
a player or storyteller doesn’t like the way something 
went and wants to go back and play it over again or 
adjust it. This shouldn’t be used to merely reroll dice, 
but any other reason is fine.
Pause (II). The pause command is used when a 
player or storyteller wants to continue playing but 
needs a break before doing so.
Continue (>). The continue command is used when 
a break is ending and the player is ready to resume the 
game session.
Fast Forward (>>). The fast forward command is 
used when a player or storyteller wants to skip to the 
next scene, either because something has come up 
that is uncomfortable in this scene or to control the 
pacing.
Finally, after the game session is over, take some 
time to talk about what everyone liked and what could 
have gone better. Adjust content ratings and other 
safety tools, as needed. As before, there should be no 
pressure to divulge why a player or storyteller wants a 
change.
The film analogy is just one suite of safety tools. 
Feel free to use any other that works for everyone 
at your table. By using safety tools, you respect the 
people at your table and foster an environment where 
everyone can consistently have fun.

T
he diversity of peoples throughout 
the multiverse is staggering. You 
can find everything from resilient 
dwarves to otherworldly elves to 
diminutive halflings to versatile 
humans, and you’ve still only 
scratched the surface. All sentient 
creatures who look more or less human in silhouette 
are collectively called a simple word—people. People 
come in diverse colors, sizes, and body types. Since 
they are sentient, they determine their own morals and 
worldview, no matter their biology.
In Those Who Wander, you select any two birth 
parents (storyteller permitting) from whom you 
inherit your innate and basic physiological traits. 
You cannot select the same birth parent twice unless 
otherwise stated, though you can choose two different 
birth parents from the same parentage. For example, 
you cannot choose one birth parent to be Elven Birth 
Parent I and the second birth parent to be the same, 
but the second birth parent can be Elven Birth Parent 
II. If your birth parents are of different parentages, you 
can decide which option, I or II, you want for either 
parent. For example, you can choose Elven Birth 
Parent I and Dwarven Birth Parent I.

backgrounds.content:
19
Chapter 3: Backgrounds
W
hat you did before becoming 
an adventurer was more than a 
job. It was a way of life. Your 
background represents your 
upbringing, culture, society, 
and profession all rolled into 
one. Your birth parents passed 
on your physiological traits, while your background 
is everything you learned as you grew up and started 
adult life.
Were those who raised you gnomish pilgrims? Did 
you apprentice for a blacksmith, or even a wizard? Did 
study come easily to you, or did you find you valued 
the strength of your arm or your uncanny aim more?
No matter your birth parents, you can choose 
any one background. Your background grants many 
features, since your formative years left a deep 
impression on you.
Ability Increase
How you spent your young life improved you in 
noticeable ways. Every background increases one or 
more of your abilities.
Proficiencies
You can gain proficiencies in saving checks, skills, 
and tools. You can add your proficiency bonus when 
rolling a check that uses a saving check, skill, or tool 
with which you are proficient.
Languages
Languages are learned. When given a choice, ask your 
storyteller which languages exist in your campaign 
setting. The language can be spoken or signed. Deaf 
characters can also choose Visual Vernacular as one of 
their languages.
Make sure that sign languages are not simply 
nonverbal counterparts to spoken languages in 
your world. To use a real-world example, American 
Sign Language, British Sign Language, and Irish 
Sign Language are all distinct languages though the 
countries where these sign languages are share one 
predominant spoken language.
Equipment
You start your adventuring career with the equipment 
you have accrued over the course of your life to this 
point. You might also have some money or other assets 
at your disposal, represented by your wealth score. For 
more information about wealth scores, see chapter 6, 
“Equipment.”

You were raised in religious seclusion, where you 
studied the teachings of a deity and worked toward 
discovering new wonders about them and the higher 
planes.

increases by 1. 
Saving Checks. You are proficient in Intelligence and

Environment, Insight, Medicine, Persuasion, and

You were raised or trained by mages, and as a result, 
you know some rudimentary magic.

Saving Checks. You are proficient in Intelligence and

Skills. You are proficient in three skills from among

You’ve spent a lot of time around the heavy sounds

your back, making you learned in the ways of metal 
smithing.
Ability Increase. Your Health increases by 1. In

diabolist.content:
You were raised by or joined a cult of devil 
worshippers or have some other connection to the 
Nine Hells.

thaumaturgy cantrip. When you take

The open road has always called to you, and you

heirlooms.content:

Chapter 4: Heirlooms
I
t’s not uncommon for an adventurer 
to pick up a seemingly insignificant 
object only to later discover its 
important role in their story. An 
heirloom is a bauble, trinket, weapon, 
or armor that proves to be more than 
it seems.
At first, an heirloom seems to be typical of its kind. 
A Staff of the Martialist is just a stick. A Soothsayer Orb 
is just a marble. Or is it? As the heirloom spends time 
with you, its powers and personality awaken.
Attunement
You must attune to an heirloom to use its properties 
(see chapter 10, “Magic Items”), and an heirloom 
takes up one of your three attunement slots.
Proficiencies
All heirlooms grant one or more proficiencies. If you 
would gain the same skill or tool proficiency from 
two different sources, you can choose a different 
proficiency of the same kind (skill or tool) instead.
Properties
An heirloom grants you a property with each step you 
take, sharing more of its distinctive power with you. 
Record the heirloom property on your character sheet 
at the same time as you record your new step feature 
(see the next chapter).
Though rare, with storyteller permission, you can 
lose, obtain, or swap heirlooms. In these unusual 
circumstances, you lose any heirloom properties 
from an heirloom you abandon or lose. If you gain a 
new heirloom, you gain access to all of the heirloom 
properties available to a character with your number 
of steps taken.
Loyal
If an heirloom you are attuned to is lost or stolen, it 
returns to you by unknown means by the next dawn, 
dusk, or midnight (as thematically appropriate).
Creating an Heirloom
If you wish to create your own custom heirloom, 
follow these guidelines:
Each heirloom grants one or more proficiencies, 
such as a skill, tool, saving check, or weapon or armor 
proficiency. Some may also grant fluency in a new 
language.
The 1st-step property should provide no mechanical 
advantage beyond what a mundane weapon, armor, 
or item would grant. Each of the heirloom properties 
from steps 2 to 4 should provide a benefit equivalent 
to that of a common magic item. Each of the heirloom 
properties from steps 5 to 10 should provide a benefit 
equivalent to that of an uncommon magic item. Step 
11 and each of the heirloom properties from steps 13 
to 16 should provide a benefit equivalent to that of a 
rare magic item. Step 12 is reserved for the Sentience 
property at which point an heirloom’s personality 
reveals itself. Each of the heirloom properties from 
steps 17 to 19 should provide a benefit equivalent to 
that of a very rare magic item. The capstone property 
that comes at step 20 should be equivalent to that of a 
legendary magic item.
At character creation, choose one of the 
options below:

armor_of_the_elements.content:
This multicolored breastplate is dented and beat up, 
with nicks and scouring all over it.
Proficiencies. If you choose Armor of the Elements 
as your heirloom, you gain proficiency with light, 
medium, and heavy armor. In addition, you are fluent 
in Primordial.
Variant: No Heirlooms
If you want to run an especially difficult or gritty campaign, you 
can run one without heirlooms or make losing one permanent. If 
you do, consider granting each heirloom-less character an extra 
armor, skill, tool, or weapon proficiency of the player’s choice.

Once you take your 15th step, the summoned 
elemental’s CS increases to 5.
Elemental Flames
Once you take your 10th step, you can cast fireball 
as a 3rd-level spell without expending a spell slot or 
material components. Once you cast the spell in this 
way, you cannot use this property again until after the 
next dawn.
Sentience
Once you take your 12th step, the Armor of Elements 
reveals itself as sentient, with an Intelligence of +1, a 
Wisdom of +2, and a Presence of +2. The armor can 
hear out to a range of 90 feet and can communicate 
with you telepathically in a voice that is light and 
androgynous. While you’re attuned to it, it knows 
every language you know.
Elemental Lightning
Once you take your 13th step, you can cast lightning 
bolt as a 4th-level spell without expending a spell slot 
or material components. Once you cast the spell in 
this way, you cannot use this property again until the 
next dawn.
Elemental Frost
Once you take your 16th step, you can cast cone of 
cold as a 5th-level spell without expending a spell slot 
or material components. Once you cast the spell in 
this way, you cannot use this property again until the 
next dawn.
Elemental Redirection
Once you take your 19th step, when you are the target 
of an attack that inflicts acid, cold, fire, lightning, or 
thunder damage, you can redirect the damage to hit 
your attacker.
If the attack hits, you can inflict half the damage 
on the attacker. If it misses you, you can redirect the 
full damage. Damage redirected in this way ignores 
immunities and resistances.
Storm of the Elements
Once you take your 20th step, you can speak or sign 
a command word as an action, and summon a storm 
cloud churning with elemental energy centered on 
you and spreading to a radius of 360 feet. This storm 
cloud lasts for 5 rounds and behaves differently each 
round. You are immune to the effects of the storm and 
these effects happen at the start of your turn. Once 
you use this property you cannot use it again until the 
next dawn.
Round 1. Thunder rolls all around you. Each 
creature under the storm cloud must make a Health 
saving check or suffer 8d6 thunder damage on a 
failed check and half as much damage as on a success. 
Creatures that can hear that fail are disoriented. The 
disoriented target can repeat the saving check at the 
end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on 
a success. Otherwise, the effect ends when the storm 
disappears.
Round 2. Burning acid rain pours violently out 
of the cloud. Each creature under the storm cloud 
must make an Agility saving check, suffering 8d6 acid 
damage on a failed check and half as much damage on 
a success.
Round 3. Bolts of lightning crackle and strike the 
ground. Each creature under the storm cloud must 
make an Agility saving check, suffering 8d6 lightning 
damage on a failed check and half as much damage on 
a success. 
Round 4. The air and rain get colder, almost 
freezing. Each creature under the storm cloud must 
make a Health saving check, suffering 8d6 cold 
damage on a failed check and half as much damage on 
a success.
Round 5. Spheres of flame pour from the cloud. 
Each creature under the storm cloud must make an 
Agility saving check, suffering 8d6 fire damage on a 
failed check and half as much damage on a success.
Axe of the Mountain 
Monarch
This axe has not a spot of rust and was forged with an 
ancient craftsmanship you don’t recognize.
Proficiencies. If you choose the Axe of the Mountain 
Monarch as your heirloom, you gain proficiency with 
greataxes and mauls and in the History skill.

skeletal version of itself, using the same stat block 
but with vulnerability to bludgeoning damage and 
immunity to poison damage, exhaustion, and the 
sickened condition.
If you targeted a corpse, the beast comes back as a 
zombie version of itself, using the same stat block but 
with immunity to poison damage and the poisoned 
condition and gaining the Undead Fortitude feature 
found in the zombie stat block. Once used, you 
cannot use this property again until after the next 
midnight.
Death Toll
Once you take your 4th step, when your health pool is 
emptied, each injured creature of your choice within 
10 feet of you must make a Health saving check, 
suffering 2d6 necrotic damage on a failure or half as 
much damage on a success.
The damage inflicted increases to 3d6 necrotic 
damage when you take your 9th step and to 4d6 with 
a range of 20 feet when you take your 14th step.
Greater Necromancy
Once you take your 5th step, your necromancy 
spells are empowered when wielding this horn.

prosthetic_limb_of_the_far_travelled.content:
C h a p t e r 4 : H e i r l o o m s
45
Keep Clean
Adventuring can take a toll on your prosthetic limb. 
Scratches and scuffs are common on artificial hands 
and feet after long journeys. Once you take your 2nd 
step, the device can be cleaned at will as if casting the 
prestidigitation spell, and minor scuffs and scratches 
can be fixed as if casting the mending spell.
Little Help from My Friends
Once you take your 3rd step, the prosthesis can be 
used to cast the unseen servant spell. Once used, 
you can’t use this property again until you finish a 
long rest.
Phantom Sensation
Although the prosthesis lacks sensation, once you 
take your 4th step, you can use your prosthesis to 
touch a wall, floor, or object (no action required). If 
the surface or item is hot, the limb briefly appears 
red. If the surface or item is cold, the limb briefly 
appears blue. This does not prevent the effects of cold 
or fire damage that may come from interacting with a 
dangerous area or object.
Forge New Pathways
Once you take your 5th step, with a phantasmal 
shimmer, the prosthesis can be used to cast the misty 
step spell. Once used, you can’t use this property again 
until you finish a long rest.
Put Up Your Feet
Once you take your 6th step, you and your prosthesis 
have become synchronized to your body’s need to 
rest. After removing the limb for 1 minute, you gain 
a second pool of health with a depth of 1d8 plus your 
number of steps taken.
This depth increases to 3d8 plus your number of 
steps taken once you take your 19th step.
Sense What Isn’t There
The prosthesis is cautious of hidden things behind 
walls or under floors. Once you take your 7th step, it 
causes you to itch ever so slightly in warning. You can 
use an action to detect secret doors, traps, or invisible 
creatures within 10 feet of you. This ability lasts for 10 
minutes.
Once used, you can’t use this property again until 
you finish a short or long rest.
Once you take your 14th step, you can use this 
property at will.
Recognizing Fall Hazards
Though you can’t feel through your prosthetic limb, 
once you take your 8th step, you’ve adapted to 
noticing dangers in your environment that may cause 
you to fall or lose your grip. At dawn, choose to have 
advantage on either Strength or Agility saving checks 
for the next 24 hours.
Protective Resistance
Your prosthesis is designed for comfort of use. 
Moreover, the device is intent on providing resistance 
from damage. Once you take your 9th step, at each 
dawn, choose one among cold, fire, lightning, or 
piercing damage. You have resistance to this damage 
type for 24 hours.
Always Ready
Highly attuned to your fight-or-flight response, your 
prosthesis extends your ability to sense danger. Once 
you take your 10th step, a painless jolt of energy 
erupts through your prosthetic limb when danger is 
present. You cannot be surprised while wearing this 
device, and you have a +5 bonus to combat order.
Adaptable Defense
Once you take your 11th step, your prosthetic limb 
aids you in adapting your movements quickly to the 
environment to meet your accessibility needs. You 
gain a +2 bonus to defense.
This bonus increases to +3 once you take your 
17th step.
Sentience
Once you take your 12th step, the prosthetic limb 
reveals itself to be a sentient item with an Intelligence 
of +1, a Wisdom of +1, and a Presence of +0. It can 
hear out to a range of 90 feet. The prosthetic limb 
can communicate with you telepathically. Its voice is 
an echo of your own, but its tone is an exaggeration 
of your own emotions. It knows every language you 
know while you’re attuned to it.
Lessons Learned
The prosthetic limb remembers past injuries and 
strives to protect you from experiencing that same 
injury again. Once you take your 13th step, when 
you take damage and are not already resistant to 
the damage type, you can use your reaction to gain 
resistance to that damage type for 1 minute.

rapier_of_swashbuckling.content:
C h a p t e r 4 : H e i r l o o m s
47
Bravado
Once you take your 4th step, you inspire allies 
with your heroics when wielding the rapier. As a 
reaction, when an ally within 30 feet of you becomes 
frightened, you can have them reroll the saving check. 
They must use the second roll.
Magical
Once you take your 5th step, you gain a +1 bonus to 
attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon.
This bonus increases to +2 when you take your 11th 
step and +3 when you take your 17th step.
Dramatic Entrance
Once you take your 6th step, during the first round 
of combat, your cape billows, your rapier gleams, and 
your hair blows in the wind, even if there is nary a 
breeze. You have advantage on your first defense check 
this round.
Grieve
Once you take your 7th step, while the rapier is on 
your person and you perceive an ally fall as a result of 
their health pool being emptied, as a reaction, you can 
move toward them to a maximum of 30 feet.
Once you take your 14th step, after reaching your 
ally, you can also shed a tear that falls on them (no 
action required), thereby adding 1 drop to their 
health pool.
Derring-Do
Once you take your 8th step, when you succeed on 
an Athletics check, you can make a rapier attack with 
advantage on your next turn.
Sworn Enemy
Once you take your 9th step, you can choose a sworn 
enemy from among the creatures you have fought in 
battle that survived the encounter. You cannot choose 
more than one sworn enemy in 10 days’ time.
When you hit your sworn enemy with this weapon, 
the creature suffers an extra 3d6 damage.
The damage increases to 4d8 when you take your 
15th step.
Parry
Once you take your 10th step, while wielding the 
rapier, as a reaction, you gain a +2 bonus to your 
defense check against one reach attack that would 
hit you.
The bonus increases to +3 once you take your 17th 
step, and if the attack misses, you can make a rapier 
attack against the attacker.
Sentience
Once you take your 12th step, the Rapier of 
Swashbuckling reveals itself to be a sentient weapon 
with an Intelligence of +0, a Wisdom of −1, and a 
Presence of +2. The rapier can hear out to a range of 
90 feet and can communicate with you telepathically 
in a voice that is suave and masculine. While you’re 
attuned to it, it knows every language you know.
Humiliate
Once you take your 13th step, when you hit with 
this rapier, a target with an Intelligence score of −3 or 
higher must succeed on a Wisdom saving check (DS 
= 8 + your Presence + your proficiency bonus) or be 
frightened of you until the end of its next turn.
The target also suffers an extra 2d8 psychic damage 
once you take your 19th step.
Hover Sword
Once you take your 18th step, you can toss this magic 
sword into the air and speak or sign a command word. 
When you do so, the sword begins to hover, flies up to 
30 feet, and attacks one creature of your choice within 
5 feet of it. The sword uses your attack roll and ability 
bonus to damage rolls.
While the sword hovers once per turn, you can 
cause it to fly up to 30 feet to another spot within 30 
feet of you (no action required). As part of the sword’s 
movement, you can cause the sword to attack one 
creature within 5 feet of it.
After the hovering sword attacks for the fourth 
time, it flies up to 30 feet and tries to return to your 
hand. If you have no hand free, it falls to the ground 
at your feet. If the sword has no unobstructed path to 
you, it moves as close to you as it can and then falls 
to the ground. It also ceases to hover if you grasp it or 
move more than 30 feet away from it.
Redirect Attack
Once you take your 20th step, while wielding the 
rapier, as a reaction, you gain a +4 bonus to your 
defense check against one reach attack that would hit 
you. If the attack misses, you can redirect the enemy’s 
attack to hit another enemy within 5 feet of it.

C h a p t e r 4 : H e i r l o o m s
55
Direction
Once you take your 2nd step, you always know which 
way is north and the number of hours until the next 
dawn or dusk as long as the orb is on your person.
Theatrics
Once you take your 3rd step, while touching this orb, 
you can use an action to cast the thaumaturgy cantrip 
from it at will.
Reveal My Enemy
Once you take your 4th step, while you touch it, the 
orb glows when within 5 feet of any celestial, fiend, or 
undead that is not behind total cover. It glows yellow 
for celestial, red for fiend, and purple for undead.
While on your person and out to a range of 60 feet, 
the orb also detects the presence of any place or object 
that has been consecrated or desecrated, as with the 
hallow spell. It glows white for a consecrated place or 
turns inky black for a desecrated place.
Fortune Telling
Once you take your 5th step, you can cast augury 
using the orb as the material component. The omens 
swim into view as ghostly words or signed by ghostly 
hands inside the orb. You cannot cast augury again 
with the orb in this way until you finish a short or 
long rest. If you cast augury as a ritual with the orb, 
you can cast it as many times as you like.
Sensing
Once you take your 6th step, while the orb is on your 
person, you can use an action to cast detect magic from 
it at will.
In addition, you can correctly identify magic items, 
except artifacts and other heirlooms, by touching 
them to the orb. If you instead have a willing creature 
touch the orb, you learn what spells, if any, are 
currently affecting it.
Masks
Once you take your 7th step, while the orb is on your 
person, you can use an action to cast the disguise self 
spell from it at will. The spell lasts as long as the orb is 
on your person or until you dispel the effect.
Censer
Once you take your 8th step, when you use an action 
to speak or sign a command word, a cloud of thick 
smoke pours out in a 60-foot radius from the orb. The 
cloud’s area is heavily obscured. Each minute smoke 
emanates from the orb within the cloud, the radius 
increases by 10 feet until it reaches its maximum 
radius of 120 feet.
The cloud persists as long as the smoke emanates 
from the orb. Stopping the effect requires you to 
repeat its command word as an action. Once the orb 
stops smoking, the cloud disperses after 10 minutes. 
A moderate wind (11 to 20 miles per hour) can also 
disperse the smoke after 1 minute, and a strong wind

step and +3 when you take your 17th step.

weapon, you can inflict additional damage equal to 12

the next dawn.

with two hands) when you take your 10th step, and

two people within 15 feet of you to succeed on a 
Health saving check (DS = 10 + your Strength + your

your next turn. Once used, you can’t use this property 
again until after the next dawn.

do so, you gain a +4 bonus to your defense.

can’t use this property again until after the next dawn.

Head. The creature is either disoriented or silenced

move or take an action, not both.

must use an Action to pick it back up.

end of its next turn.

end of its next turn.

checks against the target (or it has a −2 penalty to its 
attacks) until the end of its next turn.

steps.content:
63
Chapter 5: Steps
A
n adventurer’s journey seldom 
follows a straight, predetermined 
path. A series of twists and turns, 
some gradual, some sudden, more 
accurately describes the hero’s path. 
Each step along the way leaves its 
mark even while it forever affects 
the hero.
Steps are the discrete defining choices along a hero’s 
path. There are never more than two to choose from. 
But as paths continue to divide and divide again, 
a character can’t help but to become increasingly 
distinct from their allies.
At character creation and whenever you take a step 
thereafter, select between the available step options. 
You take a new step when you accrue sufficient 
experience points (XP) or when the storyteller finds it 
a fitting spot in the campaign.

prerequisites.content:
Except for the 1st-level steps, each step has a 
prerequisite that must be met to take the step in 
question. The prerequisite is generally a particular 
previous step option.

health_pool.content:
The depth of your health pool is determined by the 
steps you take. Each step lists a Health Die (d6, d8, 
d10, etc.). The Health Die determines how much 
your health pool deepens at that step. When you take 
the step, roll the Health Die and add your Health. 
The result is the number of drops of health your 
health pool can now hold. Alternately, in place of 
rolling, you can take the average (rounded up), listed 
parenthetically, and add your Health to it. Please note 
that you should take the maximum die roll when you 
take your 1st step.
For example, a character who takes the preternatural 
step and has a Health of +1 starts the campaign 
with a health pool 7 drops deep (1 + 6). If that same 
character later takes the chosen step as their 2nd, they 
then deepen their health pool by 6 drops (1 + 5). If at 
any point, the character increases their Health to +2, 
they deepen their health pool to hold 1 drop for each 
step they’ve taken.

spellcasting.content:
If the step you have taken allows you to learn magic 
spells, you may choose any spell of the appropriate 
level, as listed. Because of the number of spell options, 
that might feel overwhelming. If it does, choose a spell 
list from appendix A to narrow your options according 
to a particular theme.

move as far away from you as it can, and it can’t 
willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It 
also can’t take reactions. For its action, it can use only 
the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that 
prevents it from moving. If there’s nowhere to move, 
the creature can use the Dodge action.

resilient.content:
3rd-step feature
Prerequisite: militant
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You gain proficiency 
with heavy armor.
In addition, you 
have a limited well of 
stamina that you draw on to protect yourself. When 
you suffer damage or take the Withdraw action, you 
can use a reaction to replenish your health pool by a 
number of drops equal to 1d10 + your steps.
Once you use this feature, you must finish a short 
or long rest before you can use it again.

sneaky.content:
3rd-step feature
Prerequisite: gritty
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You know how to strike subtly and exploit a foe’s
distraction. Once per turn, you can inflict an extra
1d6 damage to one creature you hit with an attack if
you have advantage on the attack roll. The attack must
use a finesse or a ranged weapon.
You don’t need advantage on the attack roll if
another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it,
that enemy isn’t incapacitated, and you don’t have
disadvantage on the attack roll.
The amount of the extra damage increases by 1d6 at
every other step.

untamed.content:
3rd-step feature
Prerequisite: gritty
Health Pool: 
d10 (6)
You are particularly 
familiar with natural 
environments and are adept at traveling and surviving 
outside people’s settlements. You gain proficiency in 
the Environment skill. If you are already proficient 
in it, you gain proficiency in one of the following 
skills of your choice: Animal Handling, Medicine, or 
Stealth. In addition, choose one skill in which you are 
proficient. Your proficiency bonus is doubled for any 
ability check you make that uses this skill.
While traveling in natural terrain, you gain the 
following benefits:
• Difficult terrain doesn’t slow your group’s
travel. Your group can’t become lost except by
magical means.
• Even when you are engaged in another activity
while traveling (such as foraging, navigating, or
tracking), you remain alert to danger.
• If you are traveling alone, you can move stealthily
at a normal pace.
• When you forage, you find twice as much food as
you normally would.
• While tracking other creatures, you also learn their
exact number, their sizes, and how long ago they
passed through the area.

inescapable.content:
5th-step feature
Prerequisite: ability 
improvement (4th step)
Health Pool: d6 (4)
You gain two spell slots whose level is one higher than 
your current highest slot. In addition, you learn two 
spells of the new level or lower and one cantrip of 
your choice.
If you don’t already have spellcasting, you learn two 
cantrips of your choice, gain two 1st-level spell slots 
and learn two 1st-level spells of your choice. Choose 
one from among Intelligence, Wisdom, or Presence. 
This is your spellcasting ability.
Additionally, your damaging cantrips affect even 
creatures that avoid the brunt of the effect. When 
a creature succeeds on a saving check against your 
cantrip, the creature suffers half the cantrip’s damage 
(if any) but no additional effect from the cantrip.
Proficiency Bonus. Your proficiency bonus 
increases to +3.
Spellcasting Focus. You can use your heirloom as a 
spellcasting focus for your spells.

swift.content:
5th-step feature
Prerequisite: ability 
improvement (4th step)
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You can attack twice, 
instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action 
on your turn.
If you are not already proficient, you gain 
proficiency with simple weapons and light armor. 
In addition, you can roll a d4 in place of the normal 
damage of your unarmed strike, or if you already 
could, the damage of your unarmed strike increases 
by 1d4 and your unarmed strikes count as magical for 
the purpose of overcoming resistance and immunity to 
nonmagical attacks and damage.
Proficiency Bonus. Your proficiency bonus 
increases to +3.

athletic.content:
6th-step feature
Prerequisite: swift
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You can add half your proficiency bonus (round up) to 
any Strength, Agility, or Health check you make that 
doesn’t already use your proficiency bonus.
In addition, when you make a running long jump, 
the distance you can cover increases by a number of 
feet equal to your Strength modifier.
If you are not already proficient, you gain 
proficiency with martial weapons, medium armor, and 
shields.

attuned.content:
6th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
inescapable
Health Pool: d6 (4)
You gain a spell slot whose level is equal to your 
current highest slot, and you learn one spell of a level 
for which you have spell slots. 
In addition, choose one of the following damage 
types: acid, cold, fire, lightning, necrotic, poison, 
psychic, radiant, thunder. When you cast a spell that 
inflicts damage of the chosen type, you can add your 
spellcasting ability to one damage roll of that spell. 
Moreover, you can use an action to gain resistance to 
that damage type for 1 hour.
Once you use the resistance benefit of this feature, 
you cannot use it again until you finish a short or 
long rest.

honed.content:
6th-step feature
Prerequisite: swift
Health Pool: d12 (7)
Your instincts are so 
honed that you gain a +5 bonus to combat order. 
In addition, you know how to immobilize an 
opponent through guile or force. When you hit 
another creature with a reach weapon attack, you can 
attempt a stunning strike. The target must succeed 
on a Health saving check (DS = 8 + your proficiency 
bonus + your Strength or Agility) or be stunned until 
the end of your next turn. You can use this feature a 
number of times equal to your proficiency bonus, and 
regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest.

otherworldly.content:
6th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
inescapable
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain a spell slot 
whose level is equal 
to your current 
highest slot, and you learn one spell of a level for 
which you have spell slots. 
In addition, a supernatural being has granted you a 
portion of its power. Choose two from the following 
3rd-level spells: bestow curse, clairvoyance, major image, 
remove curse, speak with dead, speak with plants. You 
can cast these two spells without expending a spell slot 
or material components. You can cast each of these 
spells once, but you can’t cast it again until you finish 
a long rest.

beastlike.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
otherworldly
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell slot whose level is one higher than 
your current highest slot. In addition, you learn two 
spells of the new level or lower.
In addition, you can use your action to magically 
assume the shape of a beast that you have encountered 
before. You can use this feature twice. You regain 
expended uses when you finish a short or long rest.
You can transform into any beast that has a 
challenge score of 1 or lower.
You can stay in a beast shape for a number of hours 
equal to half your steps (rounded down). You then 
revert to your normal form unless you expend another 
use of this feature. You can revert to your normal 
form earlier on your turn. You automatically revert if 
you fall unconscious, your health pool is emptied, or 
you die.
While you are transformed, the following 
rules apply:
•	 Your game statistics are replaced by the statistics 
of the beast, but you retain your personality, 
Intelligence, Wisdom, and Presence. You also retain 
all of your skill and saving check proficiencies, in 
addition to gaining those of the creature. If the 
creature has the same proficiency as you and its 
score in its stat block is higher than your bonus,

berserk.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: honed
Health Pool: d12 (7)
In battle, you fight 
as if in a trance. On 
your turn, you can 
enter a trance.
While trancing, you gain the following benefits if 
you aren’t wearing heavy armor:
•	 You have advantage on Strength checks and 
Strength saving checks.
•	 When you make a reach weapon attack using 
Strength, you gain a +3 bonus to the damage roll.
•	 You have resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and 
slashing damage.
•	 You can’t be enraptured or frightened while 
trancing. If you are enraptured or frightened when 
you enter your trance, the effect is suspended for 
the duration of the trance.
If you are able to cast spells, you can’t cast them or 
concentrate on them while trancing.
Your trance lasts for 1 minute. It ends early if you 
are knocked unconscious or if your turn ends and you 
haven’t attacked a hostile creature since your last turn 
or suffered damage since then. You can also end your 
trance on your turn.
Once you have tranced a number of times equal to 
your proficiency bonus, you must finish a long rest 
before you can trance again.

evasive.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: honed
Health Pool: d8 (5)
Your instinctive 
agility lets you dodge 
out of the way of 
certain area effects, 
such as a blue dragon’s lightning breath or a fireball 
spell. When you are subjected to an effect that allows 
you to make an Agility saving check to suffer only half 
damage, you instead suffer no damage if you succeed 
on the saving check, and only half damage if you fail.

healing.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
otherworldly
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than your 
current highest slot. In addition, you learn two spells 
of the new level or lower.
The healing spells you cast on others heal you as 
well. When you cast a spell of 1st level or higher that 
adds drops to another creature’s health pool, you 
replenish a number of drops to your own health pool 
equal to 2 + the spell’s level.

Healing

indefatigable.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: athletic
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You can push 
yourself beyond 
your normal limits 
for a moment. On 
your turn, you can 
take one additional 
action. Once you use this feature, you must finish a 
short or long rest before you can use it again.
In addition, while you are wearing armor, you gain 
a +1 bonus to defense.

mystical.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
attuned
Health 
Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than your current highest slot. In addition, 
you learn two spells of the new level or lower.
You learn how to empower your words with arcane 
might to distract and confuse your opponents or 
bolster your allies. When a creature that you can 
perceive within 60 feet of you attacks, you can use 
your reaction to roll a d8 and add the result to your 
defense or subtract the result from the damage the 
creature inflicts. You can choose to use this feature 
after you make your check, but before the storyteller 
determines whether the defense check succeeds or 
fails, or before the creature inflicts its damage.
Alternately, you can subtract the result of your 
d8 roll from a creature’s ability check, but before 
the storyteller determines whether the ability check 
succeeds or fails. The creature is immune if it can’t 
hear you.
You can use this feature a number of times equal to 
your proficiency bonus and regain all expended uses 
when you finish a short or long rest.

protective.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: athletic
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You gain two spell 
slots whose level is 
equal to your current highest slot, and two spell slots 
whose level is one higher than your current highest 
slot. In addition, you learn two spells of the new level 
or lower.
If you don’t already have spellcasting, you gain 
two 1st-level spell slots and learn one 1st-level 
spell. Choose from among Intelligence, Wisdom, or 
Presence. This is your spellcasting ability.
Moreover, whenever you or a friendly creature 
within 10 feet of you must make a saving check, the 
creature gains a bonus to the saving check equal to 
your spellcasting ability bonus (with a minimum 
bonus of +1). You must be conscious to grant 
this bonus.

precise.content:
7th-step feature
Prerequisite: attuned
Health Pool: d6 (4)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than your 
current highest slot. In addition, you learn two spells 
of the new level or lower.
You can create pockets of relative safety within 
the effects of your spells. When you cast a spell that 
affects other creatures that you can perceive, you can 
choose a number of them equal to 1 + the spell’s level. 
The chosen creatures automatically succeed on their 
saving checks against the spell, and they suffer no 
damage if they would normally suffer half damage on 
a successful check.

unseen.content:
10th-step feature
Prerequisite: brutal
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You are adept at 
staying out of sight 
and out of mind. You have advantage on an Agility 
(Stealth) check if you move no more than half your 
speed on the same turn.
In addition, you can spend 1 minute creating 
camouflage for yourself. You must have access to fresh 
mud, dirt, plants, soot, and other naturally occurring 
materials with which to create your camouflage.
Once you are camouflaged in this way, you can try 
to hide by pressing yourself up against a solid surface, 
such as a tree or wall, that is at least as tall and wide 
as you are. You gain a +10 bonus to Agility (Stealth) 
checks as long as you remain there without moving or 
taking actions. Once you move or take an action or a 
reaction, you must camouflage yourself again to gain 
this benefit.

slot whose level is one higher than your current

You can add your spellcasting ability bonus to one 
damage roll of any evocation spell you cast.

fervent.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
indomitable
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
equal to your current 
highest slot, and three spell slots whose level is one 
higher than your current highest slot. In addition, you 
learn two spells of the new level or lower.
If you don’t already have spellcasting, you gain 
two 1st-level spell slots and learn one 1st-level 
spell. Choose from among Intelligence, Wisdom, or 
Presence. This is your spellcasting ability.
Choose necrotic or radiant damage. You are so 
suffused with supernatural might that all your reach 
weapon strikes carry power with them. Whenever you 
hit a creature with a reach weapon, the creature suffers 
an extra 1d8 of the chosen damage type.

fortunate.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: elect
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than 
your current highest 
slot. In addition, you learn one spell of the new level 
or lower.
You can call on a higher power to alter fate in your 
favor. When you make an ability check or a saving 
check, you can use this feature to add a d10 to your 
check. You can do so after the initial roll but before 
any of the check’s effects occur.
Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again 
until you finish a short or long rest.

injurious.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: unseen
Health Pool: d10 (6)
You are proficient in 
dealing with multiple 
foes at once. Choose 
one of the following 
benefits:
• You can use your action to make a ranged attack
against any number of creatures within 10 feet
of a point you can perceive within your weapon’s
range. You must have ammunition for each target,
as normal, and you make a separate attack roll for
each target
• You can use your action to make a reach attack
against any number of creatures within 5 feet of
you, with a separate attack roll for each target.

intercessory.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: elect
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than 
your current highest 
slot. In addition, 
you learn one spell 
of the new level or lower.
You can call on a higher power to intervene on your 
behalf when your need is great.
Imploring the power’s aid requires you to use your 
action. Describe the assistance you seek, and roll 
percentile dice. If you roll a number equal to or lower 
than your number of steps, the power intervenes. The 
storyteller chooses the nature of the intervention; 
the effect of any spell or step feature would be 
appropriate.
If the power intervenes, you can’t use this feature 
again for 7 days. Otherwise, you can use it again after 
you finish a long rest.
At your 20th step, your call for intervention 
succeeds automatically, no roll required.

intimidating.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
indomitable
Health Pool: d12 (7)
You can use your 
action to frighten 
someone with your 
menacing presence. 
When you do so, 
choose one creature that you can perceive within 30 
feet of you. If the creature can perceive you, it must 
succeed on a Wisdom saving check (DS = 8 + your 
proficiency bonus + your Strength or Presence) or be 
frightened of you until the end of your next turn. On 
subsequent turns, you can use your action to extend 
the duration of this effect on the frightened creature 
until the end of your next turn. This effect ends if the 
creature ends its turn out of line of sight or more than 
60 feet away from you.
If the creature succeeds on its saving check, you 
can’t use this feature on that creature again for 
24 hours.

nimble.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: unseen
Health Pool: d8 (5)
When an attacker 
that you can perceive 
hits you with an 
attack, you can use 
your reaction to halve the attack’s damage against you.

spellbroken.content:
11th-step feature
Prerequisite: 
sorcerous
Health Pool: d8 (5)
You gain one spell 
slot whose level is 
one higher than your 
current highest slot. 
In addition, you 
learn one spell of the new level or lower.
You learn how to break mind-influence effects 
through arcane empowered words or sounds. As an 
action, you can channel your preferred technique 
until the end of your next turn. During that time, you 
and any friendly creatures within 30 feet of you have 
advantage on saving checks against being frightened or 
enraptured, and when you use this ability any friendly 
creature currently frightened or enraptured can 
immediately make a saving check to end the effect. A 
creature must be able to hear you to gain this benefit. 
Your channel ends early if you are incapacitated or if 
you voluntarily end it (no action required).

spell of the new level or lower.
You gain the ability to magically manifest a pair of 
wings from your back, gaining a flying speed equal to 
your current speed. You can create these wings on your 
turn. They last until you dismiss them on your turn.
You can’t manifest your wings while wearing armor

When you hit a creature with an attack, you can 
use this feature to instantly transport the target 
through another plane of existence of your choice. The 
creature disappears and hurtles through an unnatural 
landscape.
At the end of your next turn, the target returns 
to the space it previously occupied, or the nearest 
unoccupied space. If the target is not a native creature 
to that plane, it suffers 10d10 psychic damage as it 
reels from its experience.
Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again

Health Pool: d8 (5)

slot whose level is 
one higher than your 
current highest slot.

one spell of the new level or lower.
Moreover, you receive the boon of a higher power. 
Choose from one of the following options:
• You can cast hold creature at will—targeting a
celestial, fiend, or elemental—without expending a
spell slot or material components. You must finish a
long rest before you can use this invocation on the
same creature again.
• You can cast alter self at will, without expending a
spell slot.
• You can cast arcane eye at will, without expending a
spell slot.
• You can perceive the true form of any shapechanger
or creature concealed by illusion or transmutation
magic while the creature is within 30 feet of you
and within your perception.

wealth.content:
No matter how you measure wealth—coins, livestock, 
property, land, or your good name—it can matter 
a great deal to characters. Whether or not you can 
acquire better armor, a deadlier weapon, or even a 
stronghold on a plot of land depends on it. At the 
same time, figuring out conversion rates, the exact 
number of coins in your purse, or how many copper 
pieces for a meal at the tavern might be a level of 
realism you don’t want in a social game among friends.

wealth_score.content:
Money and collateral is abstracted in-game with a 
wealth score. Your wealth score is an approximate 
measure of the coin and barterable goods at your 
character’s disposal. The higher the wealth score, the 
richer you are. Generally, a 1st-step character starts 
with a wealth score of 1, though some backgrounds 
or other starting character options may increase your 
wealth score beyond that.
Otherwise, your wealth score increases when 
you find a treasure chest full of gold, enjoy success 
in several nights of high-stakes gambling, receive 
a handsome payout from an investment, work for 
wages, collect a bounty, or receive a reward. Your 
wealth might not look like a pile of coins. You might 
invest it in or receive land or property or amass a 
valuable collection instead. It might not even be 
tangible. As your fame grows, you might be able 
to borrow money or goods based solely on your 
reputation. The storyteller will let you know when an 
in-game achievement increases your wealth score.

purchasing_goods_or_services.content:
Many characters enjoy shopping in an open-air market 
or local shop. Others look to construct or buy their 
own tavern, sailing ship, or even castle. Simply put, 
any purchasable item or service has a price. Whenever 
a character makes a purchase, they compare their 
wealth score to the item or service’s value score.
If the value score is lower than the character’s wealth 
score, the adventurer can make the purchase. If the 
value score is equal to the wealth score, the character 
can still make the purchase, but the item or service is 
so costly that doing so lowers their wealth score by 1. 
If the value score is greater than the wealth score, the 
price is so prohibitively high that the character must 
raise their wealth score before making the purchase.
For example, a 1st-step character with a wealth score 
of 1 can easily get a room for the night and a meal of 
bread and cheese. Both of those purchases have a value 
score of 0. But if the same character then tries to buy 
a shortsword, which has a value of 1, the purchase 
lowers their wealth score by 1, leaving the character 
broke and unable to buy anything else until they raise 
their wealth score again.
Selling an item with a value score higher than your 
current wealth score increases your wealth score. The 
amount of increase is equal to half the difference 
between the two scores (rounded up), unless the 
storyteller deems otherwise.
Variant Rule: Counting Coins
If you prefer to know exactly how much you have rattling around 
in your coin purse or the exact price down to the copper the 
merchant is selling their wares for, use the following table to

armor.content:
Fantasy gaming worlds are a vast tapestry made 
up of many different cultures, each with its own 
technologies. For this reason, adventurers have access 
to a variety of armor types, ranging from leather armor 
to chain mail to costly plate armor, with several other 
kinds of armor in between. The Armor table collects 
the most commonly available types of armor found 
in the game and separates them into three categories: 
light armor, medium armor, and heavy armor. Many 
warriors supplement their armor with a shield.
The Armor table shows the cost, weight, and other 
properties of the common types of armor worn in 
fantasy gaming worlds.
Armor Proficiency. Almost anyone can put on a 
suit of armor or strap a shield to an arm. Only those 
proficient in the armor’s use know how to wear it 
effectively, however. You might gain proficiency with 
certain types of armor at character creation. If you 
wear armor that you lack proficiency with, you have 
disadvantage on any ability check, saving check, or 
attack check that involves Strength or Agility, and you 
can’t cast spells.
Defense Bonus. Armor protects its wearer from 
attacks. The armor (and shield) you wear determines 
your defense bonus.
Light Armor. If you wear light armor, you add your 
Agility to the base number from your armor type to 
determine your defense bonus.
Medium Armor. If you wear medium armor, you 
add your Agility, to a maximum of +2, to the base 
number from your armor type to determine your 
defense bonus.
Heavy Armor. Heavy armor doesn’t let you add 
your Agility to your defense bonus, but a negative 
number for Agility doesn’t apply to your defense 
bonus either.
Heavier armor interferes with the wearer’s ability to 
move quickly, stealthily, and freely. If the Armor table 
shows “Str +1” or “Str +2” in the Strength column for 
an armor type, the armor reduces the wearer’s speed 
by 10 feet unless the wearer has a Strength equal to or 
higher than the listed Strength.
Stealth. If the Armor table shows “Disadvantage” 
in the Stealth column, the wearer has disadvantage on 
Agility (Stealth) checks.
Shields. A shield is made from wood or metal and is 
carried in one hand. Wielding a shield increases your 
defense bonus by 2. You can benefit from only one 
shield at a time.
Slots. Many pieces of armor only take up 1 item 
slot of your carrying capacity. Heavier pieces take up 2 
or even 3 slots.

Agility for the attack check and damage roll. You must 
use the same ability for both.
Lengthy. This weapon adds 5 feet to your reach

Light. A light weapon is small and easy to handle,

weapons.
Loading. Because of the time required to load this 
weapon, you can fire only one piece of ammunition 
from it when you use an action or reaction to fire 
it, regardless of the number of attacks you can 
normally make.
Range. A weapon that can be used to make a 
ranged attack has a range in parentheses after the 
ammunition or thrown property. The range lists two 
numbers. The first is the weapon’s normal range in 
feet, and the second indicates the weapon’s long range. 
When attacking a target beyond normal range, you 
have disadvantage on the attack roll. You can’t attack a 
target beyond the weapon’s long range.
Special. A weapon with the special property has 
unusual rules governing its use, explained in the 
weapon’s description (see “Special Weapons” later in 
this section).
Thrown. If a weapon has the thrown property, you 
can throw the weapon to make a ranged attack. If the 
weapon is a reach weapon, you use the same ability 
for that attack check and damage roll that you would 
use for a reach attack with the weapon. For example, 
if you throw a handaxe, you use your Strength, but if 
you throw a dagger, you can use either your Strength 
or your Agility, since the dagger has the finesse 
property.
Two-Handed. This weapon requires two hands 
when you attack with it.
Unwieldy. Small creatures have disadvantage on 
attack checks with unwieldy weapons. An unwieldy 
weapon's proportions make it too difficult for a Small 
creature to use effectively.
Versatile. This weapon can be used with one or two 
hands. A damage value in parentheses appears with the 
property—the damage when the weapon is used with 
two hands to make a reach attack.
Improvised Weapons
Sometimes characters don’t have their weapons 
and have to attack with whatever is at hand. An 
improvised weapon includes any object you can wield 
in one or two hands, such as broken glass, a table leg, 
a frying pan, a wagon wheel, or a dead giant rat.
Often, an improvised weapon is similar to an actual 
weapon and can be treated as such. For example, a 
table leg is akin to a club. At the storyteller’s option, 
a character proficient with a weapon can use a 
similar object as if it were that weapon and use their 
proficiency bonus.
An object that bears no resemblance to a weapon 
deals 1d4 damage (the storyteller assigns a damage 
type appropriate to the object). If a character uses a 
ranged weapon to make a reach attack, or throws a 
reach weapon that does not have the thrown property, 
it also deals 1d4 damage. An improvised thrown 
weapon has a normal range of 20 feet and a long range 
of 60 feet.
Silvered Weapons
Some nonplayer creatures that have immunity or 
resistance to nonmagical weapons are susceptible to 
silver weapons, so cautious adventurers invest extra 
coin to plate their weapons with silver. The process of 
silvering a single weapon or ten pieces of ammunition 
has a value score of 3. This cost represents not only the 
price of the silver, but the time and expertise needed 
to add silver to the weapon without making it less 
effective.
Special Weapons
Weapons with special rules are described here.
Lance. You have disadvantage when you use a lance 
to attack a target within 5 feet of you. Also, a lance 
requires two hands to wield when you aren’t mounted.
Net. A Large or smaller creature hit by a net is 
restrained until it is freed. A net has no effect on 
creatures that are formless, or creatures that are Huge 
or larger. A creature can use its action to make a DS 
10 Strength check, freeing itself or another creature 
within its reach on a success. Inflicting 5 slashing 
damage to the net (defense score 10) also frees the 
creature without harming it, ending the effect and 
destroying the net.
When you use an action or reaction to attack with 
a net, you can make only one attack regardless of the 
number of attacks you can normally make.
